title: How to Disagree About Politics With People You Love
excerpt: We are losing marriages, friendships, and family over elections, at a rate our grandparents would not recognize. Here is how to keep your convictions and keep your people.
body:
Something has gone wrong when a family stops speaking over a vote, when a friendship of decades ends over a candidate, when a holiday table becomes a theater of war. We are losing the people we love over politics at a rate that would have baffled our grandparents, who managed to disagree about elections and still pass the potatoes. The wider culture has taught us that those who differ politically are not merely wrong but dangerous, and we have let that lesson into our homes.

Christians have caught the same disease, and it is killing our witness, because a faith that cannot stay in the room with people who disagree has nothing to offer a divided world. Jesus kept company with a zealot who wanted Rome overthrown and a tax collector who collaborated with Rome, at the same table, in the same band of disciples. He loved them into a room together. That is the model, and it is harder than picking a side.

## Decide the relationship outranks the argument

The decisive move happens before the conversation: this person matters more to me than winning this point. If you have not settled that in advance, the heat of the moment will settle it for you, and you will choose the win and lose the person. Most political arguments are not actually about policy. They are about whether each person feels respected and whether each one feels safe. Decide that the people you love will leave the conversation feeling loved even if neither of you moved an inch, and you have already kept what matters.

This is not cowardice and it is not mushiness. It is the refusal to sacrifice a real human being on the altar of a point you could have made another way, or never needed to make at all.

## Find the fear or the value underneath

Underneath almost every political position is a fear or a wound or a value worth honoring. The relative whose politics alarm you is usually protecting something they love, a way of life, a vulnerable group, a moral order they fear is collapsing. Ask why they hold what they hold, and listen for the thing underneath. Proverbs says to answer before listening is folly and shame, and most of our political arguments are folly and shame by that definition, because we are loading the rebuttal while they are still talking.

Try stating their view back so well that they say, yes, that is what I mean. The person who feels truly understood can tolerate disagreement. The person who feels caricatured cannot, and most of our family fights are fights between two caricatures, neither of which anyone actually holds.

## Hold conviction, refuse contempt

You can hold a political conviction firmly and refuse contempt entirely. The culture insists these are the same thing. They are not. To disagree is to think someone is wrong. To hold them in contempt is to think they are beneath you, stupid or evil for disagreeing. The first is honest. The second is poison, and the people you love feel it through every polite word. I have caught contempt in my own voice while saying all the reasonable things, and the contempt is what my people heard, not the reasonableness. Repent of the contempt and the disagreement can stay in the room without ending the relationship.

## Remember neither party is your church

Here the partisan capture must be named. The reason political disagreement now feels like a rupture in a family is that politics has become an identity, almost a religion, and to differ feels like a betrayal of the tribe. The ancient Christian ethic refuses to let either party become the thing that defines belonging. Your brother who votes differently is still your brother. Your friend across the line is still your friend. Their party is not their soul, and yours is not yours. When the baptism is thicker than the ballot, you can disagree about an election and still be one family, which is exactly the witness a sorted and bitter country is quietly desperate to see.

## This week

Think of one relationship currently strained by political disagreement, and take a step toward that person that has nothing to do with the argument: a call, a meal, a kind word that says you matter more to me than this. If the topic comes up, practice stating their view back until they agree you have understood it, before you say a word in reply. And listen for your own contempt. If you find it, set it down. You can keep your convictions. Do not lose your people to them.
